text: In 1899, two lawyers from Chattanooga, Tennessee, came to see him. Benjamin Thomas and Joseph Whitehead had an idea: put Coca-Cola in bottles.
Candler wasn't impressed. Bottling was messy, and his drink was made for the soda fountain. But if they wanted to take the risk... fine.
He sold them the rights to bottle Coca-Cola across most of the United States. For one dollar. And, reportedly, he never even collected it.

That dollar built the empire. Thomas and Whitehead didn't build every plant themselves. They signed up local businessmen who paid for their own bottling plants, their own trucks and their own salesmen.
Town after town got its own Coca-Cola bottler, with its own money on the line. The company sold the syrup. The bottlers did the rest.
But success attracts copycats. Soon there were drinks with almost the same name, in almost the same bottle.

So in 1915, the bottlers asked glass makers for a bottle you could recognize in the dark... or even broken on the ground. A glass company in Terre Haute, Indiana, came back with a curvy design. The contour bottle.
